Intel (INTC) has been pulled in two directions lately. New collaborations in AI infrastructure and edge computing land alongside sharp sector swings tied to Nvidia's CEO exit, as well as fresh governance and geopolitical headlines.

Recent trading shows how conflicted investors are about Intel. The 1-day share price return of 7.52% and 7-day gain of 19.62% follow a 30-day share price decline of 39.21%. At the same time, the year-to-date share price return is 58.71% and the 1-year total shareholder return is 74.05%.

Intel now trades well below both analysts' average target and some estimates of fair value after a sharp pullback. Is that discount compensation for real execution, governance and geopolitical risks, or an overreaction?

Most Popular Narrative: 88% Undervalued

The narrative fair value for Intel sits at $500.93 versus the last close of $62.50, which points to a very large implied discount according to Suen, an investor in the Simply Wall St Community who set out a detailed thesis comparing Intel's x86 position and foundry footprint to rivals.

Compared to ARM, x86 does face an overhead penalty due to hypervisor translation on the assumption that ARM has been natively built. However, the majority of applications are not natively built (aside from webpages), which would mean ARM would suffer a significant emulation penalty in terms of performance. Additionally, even with a natively compiled binary for ARM, x86 could still come out on top due to ARM being less cache efficient, as the same application compiled for ARM generates larger code objects that could lower cache hit rate (depending on application).

Analog Devices (ADI) and NVIDIA (NVDA) are both bought for the AI data center buildout, and the better buy depends on how much of your money you want on that one bet. NVIDIA made $89 billion of its $96 billion fiscal Q2 2027 revenue from data centers. At Analog Devices, management puts its AI exposure at about 20% of the company. That share counts its ATE and data center businesses together. So what did each company tell investors in August about the quarters ahead?

Analog Devices Expects Higher Margins, NVIDIA Expects Lower

Analog Devices told investors on August 19, 2026, that it expects its adjusted gross margin to rise to about 74% in fiscal Q4 2026, up from 72.5% in fiscal Q3. Management tied the gain to a better product mix, higher volumes and its own price increase, adding that the full effect of that price increase is not yet in the fiscal Q4 outlook.

The outlook from NVIDIA moved in the opposite direction. Memory prices rose more than management expected, leading the company to reset its margin outlook. NVIDIA now expects its gross margin to bottom at 71% to 72% in fiscal Q4 2027, down from 75% in fiscal Q2. The company's own price increases only take effect in fiscal Q1 2028.

Both companies guided revenue above the quarter they had just reported, meaning the two outlooks differ on profit rather than demand. Analog Devices is raising its prices now. NVIDIA is absorbing higher memory costs until its own price increases arrive.

Where NVIDIA And Analog Devices Spend Cash

NVIDIA is backing its own customers. Management said on the August 26, 2026 call that NVIDIA has invested nearly $50 billion in frontier AI labs, and that it expects AI labs it supports with its balance sheet to make up roughly a quarter of its business next year. Management also said it knows some will call this circular financing, though it said it sees the arrangements differently. That is the cost of NVIDIA's approach: more of its growth now depends on how those labs fare.

Analog Devices spends on acquisitions and shareholders. The company paid $1.5 billion in cash for Empower Semiconductor in July 2026, and in November 2026 completed its acquisition of Alif Semiconductor for $1.35 billion in cash plus up to $200 million in contingent payments, funded with part of a $3 billion bond sale in September. Management said it returned more than all of its free cash flow over the past twelve months to shareholders. On August 1, 2026, before that bond sale, Analog Devices owed $9.12 billion against $2.32 billion in cash and short-term investments.

Intel Corp (NASDAQ:INTC) shares fell 3.49% to $60.32 at 9:35 a.m. ET in early regular-session trading on November 12 as investors questioned what NVIDIA's (NASDAQ:NVDA) leadership change means for the companies' partnership. The drop reverses part of Wednesday's 7.52% gain.

INTC GF Value chart

NVIDIA bought 214.78 million Intel shares at $23.28 each, about $5 billion, in a deal that closed on December 26, 2025, according to Invezz. The collaboration covers custom Intel x86 CPUs linked to NVIDIA platforms through NVLink and PC processors that pair NVIDIA RTX graphics chiplets with Intel CPUs, but it carries no commitment to move NVIDIA production into Intel's foundries. Intel's third-quarter revenue rose 21% to $16.5 billion and Data Center and AI sales jumped 78% to $7.3 billion, while the fourth-quarter forecast of $15 billion to $16 billion disappointed and Intel Foundry lost about $1.9 billion.

At $60.32, NVIDIA's stake is worth about $13.0 billion, a paper gain near $8 billion that a new CEO could choose to keep, trim or reframe. GuruFocus gives Intel a GF Score of 70/100, with 9/10 momentum but a GF Value Rank of 1/10. The shares trade 76.6% above the GF Value of $34.15, a "Significantly Overvalued" label, and GuruFocus shows no P/E because of losses. Momentum has outrun the model. The next test is NVIDIA's November 17 call and any comment on the Intel product roadmap.

Prediction: This Will Be Intel’s Stock Price After 1 Year (Hint: It Implies a Nice Jump)
Harsh Chauhan, The Motley Fool

NVDA

Trading disclosure

Shares of Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) delivered incredible gains to investors in the first half of 2026, but have seen significant volatility in recent months.

As it turns out, Intel stock has retreated 51% since the beginning of July. The past few days have been even more brutal for Intel investors, with the stock plunging big time following the release of its third-quarter results on Oct. 29. However, Intel's pullback could be an opportunity for savvy investors to buy a top semiconductor stock at an attractive valuation, especially given its solid upside potential.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Let's take a closer look at Intel's prospects and valuation to check how much upside it could deliver over the coming year.

Image source: Getty Images.

Intel's data center business will drive stronger growth in 2027

When Intel released its Q3 results, the company reported a solid 21% increase in revenue from the year-ago period to $16.5 billion. The company's non-GAAP earnings per share (EPS) jumped by an incredible 126% from the year-ago period to $0.52.

Intel delivered such impressive growth despite a 5% decline in revenue from its client computing and physical artificial intelligence (AI) business segment. It is worth noting that this business is a key source of revenue for Intel, accounting for nearly half its top line in Q3. The ongoing weakness in the PC market, along with Intel's market share losses to Advanced Micro Devices, explains why Chipzilla's sales in this segment dropped last quarter.

The bad news for Intel investors is that the PC market's decline is here to stay. Counterpoint Research notes that PC sales dropped by 21% last quarter, and the Q4 decline is likely to be steeper at 27%. Higher costs of memory and other components are taking a toll on this market. The positive news is that Intel expects the PC decline to ease in 2027, with unit shipments predicted to drop by 10%.

However, the biggest takeaway from Intel's quarterly report is the impressive growth in the company's data center business. Its data center and AI revenue increased by an incredible 78% from the year-ago period to $7.3 billion, helping lift the company's top and bottom lines. Looking ahead, Intel expects the data center business to sustain its solid momentum in 2027, driven primarily by the healthy demand for server central processing units (CPUs).
